title: How CNC evolved from punched-tape NC machines
summary: From holes in paper tape to conversational controls at the spindle: each era of numerical control fixed the era before it.

blocks.title: The program moved from paper to memory
blocks.body: CNC did not arrive as an invention so much as an accumulation. Each generation of numerical control kept the same promise - the machine follows a program instead of a handwheel - and fixed whatever the previous generation made painful. Walking the eras is the fastest way to understand why a modern control works the way it does.

items.title: The problem
items.detail: Complex aircraft parts needed curves no machinist could handwheel consistently. The Air Force funded work at MIT to make a milling machine follow recorded positions.

items.title: First NC demonstration
items.detail: A modified Cincinnati Hydrotel mill follows instructions from punched paper tape - positions encoded as holes, read one block at a time. The machine obeys; it does not compute.

items.title: APT and the programming bottleneck
items.detail: Writing tape by hand for every part was misery. APT, one of the first programming languages, lets a part be described geometrically and compiled into toolpaths. Programming becomes a profession.

items.title: NC spreads
items.detail: Tape readers and hardwired logic cabinets appear on shop floors. The machines are expensive, finicky, and transformative for batch aerospace work. A crashed tape reader is a stopped machine.

items.title: The C arrives
items.detail: Minicomputers get cheap enough to dedicate one to a single machine. Computer numerical control stores programs in memory, edits them at the machine, and softens the hardwired logic into software.

items.title: Microprocessors and the shop floor
items.detail: Fanuc and others put the control on chips. Drip-feeding long programs over serial lines, CRT screens, and the first canned cycles. CNC leaves the aerospace plant for the job shop.

items.title: PC-based controls and CAM
items.detail: Desktop CAD/CAM writes the toolpath; the control becomes a PC in a cabinet. Surface machining of molds and dies - impossible on tape-era hardware - becomes routine.

items.title: Conversational and connected
items.detail: Controls talk back: probing cycles measure the part in the machine, tool monitoring watches the cut, and the program flows from the network instead of a tape or a floppy. The machinist's job shifts from crank-turning to process-owning.

blocks.heading: What each era actually fixed
rows: Tape editing, tape storage, reader failures
A programming department between drawing and machine
Hardwired inflexibility, no editing at the machine
Software complexity, dependence on one computer
Cost and size of the control
Version control of programs becomes a real problem

blocks.heading: The through-line
blocks.body: Notice what never changed: a block of instructions, executed in order, moving axes to positions. G-code today would be legible to a 1960s tape programmer. The revolutions were all around the program - how it is written, stored, simulated, measured against, and corrected - not in what the machine fundamentally does when it obeys.

blocks.quote: We did not replace the machinist. We moved the machinist's judgment from the crank to the program.
